newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Vienna new share market a step on the right road.
newsitem.headline: Vienna new share market a step on the right road.

text.p: The Vienna stock exchange may take a step towards boosting liquidity when it launches a market for small firms next year but it still has some way to go to convince Austrian businesses to list shares, analysts said.

Finance Minister Viktor Klima and stock exchange president Gerhard Randa announced late on Tuesday that the new market, called Fit, would start early next year with the first listings of small and medium-sized companies in the second quarter.
"We are confident that we have taken a stride towards doubling market capitalisation over the next five years," Klima said after a stock exchange strategy group meeting.
Analysts gave a cautious welcome to the news but warned that the road ahead may be bumpy.

Without a change in Austrian attitudes towards share ownership the Vienna exchange, one of Europe's oldest but smallest, would fail to meet its target of raising market capitalisation to 600 billion schillings ($56 billion) from 300 billion, or 16 percent of gross domestic product, they said.
"I will be very surprised if it works like that. Things are not that simple," said Alfred Reisenberger, an analyst at IMI Sigeco in London.
"This is an interesting development but a lot will depend on how attractive the new market is," said Gerhard Auer, an analyst at ICE Securities in London.

Vienna's efforts to attract new listings took a knock in September when semi-conductor maker SEZ announced it planned its flotation in Zurich, citing Swiss bank placement expertise and an excellent environment for technology stocks.

Brussels' European small cap market Easdaq and the London stock exchange's Alternative Investment Market (AIM) had a head start in drumming up business among small and fast-growing east European firms, Auer noted.
Reisenberger said the Austrian government should do more to encourage domestic firms to raise capital over the stock exchange rather than turning to banks for loans.
It also needed to tackle public reluctance to buy shares. Most Austrians prefer to put their savings in the bank.
"It is easy to create a market but first the perception in Austria must change," Reisenberger said.

Stock exchange working groups will meet over the next few months to consider changes to the regulatory environment -- including tax reform and more protection for minority shareholders -- in order to promote new listings and stimulate investor demand.

But some analysts doubted there was a genuine political will to make the necessary adjustments and noted Austrian working groups were quite capable of meeting for years without reaching any conclusions.
"It sounds like lip service," said one. "The task is not difficult. All they have to do is look at Germany, Britain and the U.S. and copy the best bits."

The stock exchange also failed to deliver any firm promises on improving the quality and increasing the frequency of company reports. At present Austrian firms are not obliged to release quarterly figures and data, when it is published, is often patchy and difficult to decipher.
